idiom_name: immutable List snapshot over a private mutable buffer
implementation_notes: Scala defaults to immutable collections, so the idiom is to keep a private mutable builder - `private val _courses = mutable.ArrayBuffer.empty[Course]` - and publish an immutable value: `def courses: collection.immutable.Seq[Course] = _courses.toList`. The collections overview notes that copying functions such as `toList` 'create a snapshot of a collection at a specific moment' and that later changes to the original do not affect the copy, which is why the published type can carry the read-only guarantee. Declare the result as `immutable.Seq`/`List`, not as a root `collection.Seq`: the overview warns that a root collection 'only promises not to change the collection themselves' while the runtime value may still be a mutable buffer. Mutators addCourse/removeCourse own validation and bookkeeping.
pitfalls: `toList` copies on every read; where reads dominate and updates are rare, keep the immutable List as the single source of truth and use a `var`, or cache the snapshot and invalidate it in the mutators.
Declaring the result as `collection.Seq`/`scala.Seq` only promises the client will not mutate it - the runtime value can still be a mutable buffer; name `immutable.Seq`/`List` explicitly.

The published type is immutable, but the private buffer is still reachable from companion objects or nested code; use `private[this]` (Scala 2) or plain `private` with instance-local access (Scala 3).
Java interop sees `java.util.List` and can call add(); hand Java consumers an unmodifiable copy at that boundary.
